source.title: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
source.attribution: Benjamin Franklin, The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, Standard Ebooks, public domain

cards.title: Work on one habit at a time, not all thirteen at once
cards.body:
Franklin drew up a list of thirteen virtues he wanted to build, from temperance to humility, then found that chasing them all at once just scattered his attention. So he gave each virtue a full week of focus and let the others take their chances. Every evening he put a small black dot in a notebook grid for each slip, aiming to keep that week's line clean. Thirteen weeks made a cycle, and he could run four cycles a year.

The same logic suits habit change today: pick one behaviour, track it daily in a simple grid or app, and add the next only once the first feels automatic.
cards.quote: like him who, having a garden to weed, does not attempt to eradicate all the bad herbs at once, which would exceed his reach and his strength, but works on one of the beds at a time
cards.locator: IX. Plan for Attaining Moral Perfection ¶34
cards.apply_it: Choose one habit to focus on this week. Draw seven boxes on a card and add a dot each evening you slip.

quiz.question: Why did Franklin give each virtue its own week?
options: He believed some virtues mattered more than others
Working on everything at once spread his attention too thin
His notebook only had room for one virtue a week
A friend told him to
quiz.explanation: Like weeding one garden bed at a time, focusing on a single virtue let him see real progress instead of being overwhelmed.

cards.title: Open the day with one question and close it with another
cards.body:
Franklin's daily plan was simple: rise early, plan the day, work, break at noon to read or check his accounts, work again, then spend the evening tidying up, with music or conversation. What made it stick were two bookend questions. Each morning he asked what good he would do that day and set a resolution; each night he asked what good he had actually done and reviewed the day.

That turns a schedule into a feedback loop. A two-minute intention in the morning and a short review at night, before you reach for your phone, show you the gap between what you meant to do and what really happened.
cards.quote: Question. What good shall I do this day?
cards.locator: IX. Plan for Attaining Moral Perfection ¶47
cards.apply_it: Tonight, write one line answering: what good did I do today? Tomorrow morning, write one line for: what good will I do today?

quiz.question: Which question did Franklin ask himself every evening?
options: How much money did I make today?
Who did I meet today?
What will I eat tomorrow?
What good have I done today?
quiz.explanation: His evening question, 'What good have I done today?', paired with the morning one, 'What good shall I do this day?', and ended with a review of the day.

cards.title: Spend only on what does real good for you or others
cards.body:
Franklin's rule for frugality was short: make no expense unless it does some good, to others or to yourself; in other words, waste nothing. As a young printer still in debt, he and his wife kept a plain table and cheap furniture, and he later credited frugality and hard work for his early financial ease.

He also liked the proverb that an empty sack can't stand upright: someone always short of money finds it harder to act freely and honestly. Frugality here isn't stinginess. It's a filter that asks whether each purchase actually does good, which makes the forgotten subscriptions and impulse buys easy to cut.
cards.quote: Make no expense but to do good to others or yourself; i.e., waste nothing.
cards.locator: IX. Plan for Attaining Moral Perfection ¶13
cards.apply_it: Look over your last ten purchases. Mark the ones that did real good for you or someone else, and cancel or skip one that didn't.

quiz.question: How did Franklin define frugality?
options: Never spend money on yourself
Save half of everything you earn
Spend only on what does good for others or yourself
Always buy the cheapest option
quiz.explanation: His precept was 'Make no expense but to do good to others or yourself; i.e., waste nothing.' Spending on yourself was fine if it did real good.

cards.title: Swap 'certainly' for 'it seems to me' and people listen more
cards.body:
After a friend told him he came across as proud and overbearing in arguments, Franklin changed how he talked. He dropped words that signalled a fixed opinion, like 'certainly' and 'undoubtedly', and used softer openers such as 'I imagine' or 'it appears to me at present'. When someone said something he thought was wrong, he resisted pouncing. He first noted where their view might hold, then explained why this case seemed different.

Conversations became friendlier, his ideas met less resistance, and being wrong cost him less embarrassment. In a meeting or a heated group chat, tentative phrasing lets people change their minds without losing face.
cards.quote: The modest way in which I proposed my opinions procured them a readier reception and less contradiction; I had less mortification when I was found to be in the wrong
cards.locator: IX. Plan for Attaining Moral Perfection ¶66
cards.apply_it: In your next disagreement, start with where the other person might be right, then say 'in this case it seems to me…' before giving your view.

quiz.question: What did Franklin find when he stopped speaking dogmatically?
options: His ideas were accepted more readily
People stopped taking him seriously
He lost most of his arguments
He had to talk for longer
quiz.explanation: Modest phrasing got his opinions 'a readier reception and less contradiction', and made it easier to admit when he was wrong.

cards.title: Build a small circle that meets to sharpen each other's thinking
cards.body:
In his early twenties Franklin gathered his most curious friends, mostly tradesmen, into a club called the Junto that met every Friday evening. Each member brought questions to discuss, and every three months wrote and read out an essay. Arguing to win was against the rules: the aim was to find the truth, and blunt contradiction was even fined.

The group later pooled its books into a shared library and tested ideas that grew into real public projects. A modern version is easy: a few friends, a regular slot, a question each, and an agreement to stay curious rather than competitive. Over the years, a group like that can teach you more than many courses.
cards.quote: Our debates were to be under the direction of a president, and to be conducted in the sincere spirit of inquiry after truth, without fondness for dispute, or desire of victory
cards.locator: VII. Beginning Business in Philadelphia ¶20
cards.apply_it: Invite two or three people you learn from to a monthly coffee or call. Ask each to bring one question worth discussing.

quiz.question: What was the main rule for debates in Franklin's Junto?
options: The best speaker won a prize
Seek the truth rather than victory in argument
Only the president could speak
Members had to agree with each other
quiz.explanation: Debates were to be held 'in the sincere spirit of inquiry after truth, without fondness for dispute, or desire of victory'.

cards.title: To win over a rival, ask them for a small favour
cards.body:
A new member of the Pennsylvania assembly had spoken out against Franklin. Rather than flatter him or fight back, Franklin learned the man owned a rare book and wrote asking to borrow it. The book arrived, Franklin returned it a week later with a warm note of thanks, and the next time they met the man spoke to him kindly. They stayed friends for life.

Franklin explained it with an old maxim: someone who has done you a kindness is readier to do another than someone you have helped. A genuine, small request invites people to see themselves as on your side. It works with a cool colleague too, if the ask is sincere and easy.
cards.quote: He that has once done you a kindness will be more ready to do you another, than he whom you yourself have obliged.
cards.locator: X. Poor Richard’s Almanac and Other… ¶17
cards.apply_it: Think of someone who is cool towards you. Ask them for a small, genuine favour, such as their advice or a recommendation, and thank them properly.

quiz.question: How did Franklin win over a hostile fellow legislator?
options: He praised him in public
He did him a large favour
He asked to borrow a rare book from him
He avoided him until he calmed down
quiz.explanation: Lending the book made the man more inclined to help Franklin again: someone who has done you a kindness is readier to do another.

cards.title: Chasing an ideal you'll never reach can still make you better
cards.body:
Franklin admitted he never achieved the moral perfection he set out to reach. Order defeated him in particular: business kept breaking his schedule, and his papers stayed messy into old age. Yet he concluded that the attempt had made him a better and happier man.

He compared it to copying a model of perfect handwriting. You never match the engraved original, but your own hand improves along the way. That's a useful answer to all-or-nothing thinking. Falling short of your ideal isn't failure if trying is moving you forward; giving up because you can't be flawless is.
cards.quote: though I never arrived at the perfection I had been so ambitious of obtaining, but fell far short of it, yet I was, by the endeavour, a better and a happier man than I otherwise should have been if I had not attempted it
cards.locator: IX. Plan for Attaining Moral Perfection ¶60
cards.apply_it: Name one goal you've been tempted to drop because you keep falling short. Write down one way you're already better for trying.

quiz.question: What image did Franklin use to show the value of aiming for perfection?
options: Copying a model of perfect handwriting
A ship steering by the stars
Climbing a mountain
Building a house brick by brick
quiz.explanation: People who copy engraved handwriting never match it, but their own writing improves through the effort.

cards.title: A useful result doesn't excuse a dishonest method
cards.body:
As a boy, Franklin led his friends in building a little fishing wharf on a muddy marsh. The stones came from a pile meant for a new house, carried off at night after the workmen left. When they were caught, Franklin argued that the wharf was useful. His father's reply stuck with him for life: nothing is useful that is not honest.

It's an easy trap at any age: a shortcut seems justified because the goal is good. Franklin's father taught him to judge the means, not just the outcome.
cards.quote: though I pleaded the usefulness of the work, mine convinced me that nothing was useful which was not honest.
cards.locator: I. Ancestry and Early Youth in Boston ¶14
cards.apply_it: Think of a shortcut you've justified because the result was good. Would you be comfortable explaining the method to everyone affected?

quiz.question: What lesson did Franklin's father teach him after the stolen-stones wharf?
options: Always build with your own materials
Nothing is useful which is not honest
Work only in daylight
Leaders take the blame for followers
quiz.explanation: Franklin pleaded the wharf was useful, but his father convinced him nothing useful can be dishonest.

cards.title: Teach yourself a skill by copying a model and comparing
cards.body:
Young Franklin admired the essays in The Spectator and set out to write like them. He'd jot short notes on each sentence's meaning, wait a few days, then rewrite the essay from his notes without looking. Comparing his version with the original showed his faults. To build vocabulary he turned essays into verse and back; to learn structure he shuffled his notes and rebuilt the order.

This is deliberate practice: imitate an expert, compare honestly, fix the gaps, repeat. It works for writing, code, design or speeches.
cards.quote: Then I compared my Spectator with the original, discovered some of my faults, and corrected them.
cards.locator: II. Beginning Life as a Printer ¶6
cards.apply_it: Pick one excellent example in your field. Reproduce a short piece of it from memory, then compare and list three differences.

quiz.question: How did Franklin practise writing using The Spectator?
options: He copied the essays word for word
He paid a tutor to correct his work
He rewrote essays from his notes and compared them with the originals
He wrote letters to the editors
quiz.explanation: He made hints of each sentence, rewrote the essay later from those hints, then compared it with the original to find faults.

cards.title: Spend less on daily basics to free money and time for growth
cards.body:
At sixteen Franklin tried a vegetarian diet and offered his brother a deal: pay him half his usual board money and he'd feed himself. Eating simple meals, he saved half of even that, and spent it on books. There was a bonus: while the others went out to eat, he stayed in the empty print shop with a quick, light meal and used the rest of the break to study.

You don't need his diet to use the principle. Trimming a routine expense can fund your learning, and a short, simple lunch can buy back a slice of the day for reading or a course.
cards.quote: I presently found that I could save half what he paid me. This was an additional fund for buying books.
cards.locator: II. Beginning Life as a Printer ¶7
cards.apply_it: Find one daily spend you could simplify. Put the saving toward a book or course, and use the time saved to study it.

quiz.question: What two benefits did Franklin gain from feeding himself cheaply as an apprentice?
options: Money for books and free time to study
Better health and a promotion
A larger room and new clothes
Respect from his brother and father
quiz.explanation: He saved half his board money for books and studied in the shop while the others were out eating.

cards.title: Watch out: you can always find a reason for what you want
cards.body:
Franklin had given up eating fish, reasoning that killing them was unprovoked. Then, on a becalmed voyage, the crew fried fresh cod and it smelled wonderful. He wavered until he remembered seeing small fish in the cod's stomachs: if they eat each other, he thought, why shouldn't we eat them? He enjoyed his dinner.

He told the story against himself. Being a reasoning creature, he joked, lets you find or make a reason for anything you already want to do. Psychologists call it motivated reasoning. Noticing when your logic suspiciously matches your appetite is a useful habit.
cards.quote: So convenient a thing is it to be a reasonable creature, since it enables one to find or make a reason for everything one has a mind to do.
cards.locator: IV. First Visit to Boston ¶16
cards.apply_it: Next time you find a perfect reason to do what you already wanted, ask: would I accept this argument if it pointed the other way?

quiz.question: What was Franklin poking fun at in his fish story?
options: Sailors' cooking skills
Vegetarian diets
The habit of inventing reasons for what we already want
The cruelty of fishing
quiz.explanation: He joked that reason lets us 'find or make a reason for everything one has a mind to do'.

cards.title: Be wary of people who promise much but deliver little
cards.body:
Governor Keith flattered the teenage Franklin, promised to set him up as a printer, and sent him to London to buy equipment with letters of credit. When Franklin arrived, there were no letters and no credit. A friend explained that Keith was known for this: he wanted to please everyone, and having little to give, he gave expectations.

Some people mean well in the moment but can't follow through. Before you plan your life around a promise, look at the person's track record, ask others who know them, and get something concrete before you commit.
cards.quote: He wished to please everybody; and, having little to give, he gave expectations.
cards.locator: VI. First Visit to London ¶7
cards.apply_it: Is any plan of yours resting on someone's promise? Ask for one concrete step from them before you invest more.

quiz.question: How did Franklin explain Governor Keith's broken promises?
options: Keith had been robbed
Keith wanted to please everyone and, having little to give, gave expectations
Keith disliked Franklin
Keith forgot because he was busy
quiz.explanation: Franklin concluded Keith habitually gave expectations because he had little real help to give.

cards.title: Small daily spending habits quietly eat your wages
cards.body:
In a London printing house Franklin drank only water, while his fellow pressmen drank strong beer six times a day, believing it made them strong. He noticed the cost more than anything: his companion owed four or five shillings from his wages every Saturday for drink, an expense Franklin simply didn't have. He concluded that such habits kept the men permanently behind.

The modern versions are daily coffees, snacks, airtime top-ups, betting slips or delivery fees. Each is small; together, they can swallow a real share of your pay.
cards.quote: He drank on, however, and had four or five shillings to pay out of his wages every Saturday night for that muddling liquor; an expense I was free from.
cards.locator: VI. First Visit to London ¶16
cards.apply_it: Track every small daily purchase for one week. Total it, multiply by 52, and decide if it's worth that yearly price.

quiz.question: What did Franklin notice about his fellow pressmen's beer habit?
options: It made them work faster
Their employer paid for it
It cost them a large slice of their weekly wages
It was cheaper than water
quiz.explanation: His companion paid four or five shillings out of his wages every week for drink, which kept the men behind.

cards.title: Choose your battles with people you see every day
cards.body:
When Franklin moved to the compositors' room in a London print shop, they demanded a fee for drinks. He thought it unfair, and his employer agreed. But for weeks his type was mixed up and his pages jumbled whenever he stepped away. In the end he paid, concluding it was foolish to stay on bad terms with people you must live and work beside.

Once on good terms, he gained influence and even changed some of their rules. Sometimes the small price of fitting in buys the standing to improve things later.
cards.quote: I found myself obliged to comply and pay the money, convinced of the folly of being on ill terms with those one is to live with continually.
cards.locator: VI. First Visit to London ¶17
cards.apply_it: Is there a minor dispute with a colleague, neighbour or housemate that costs you more peace than it's worth? Consider settling it.

quiz.question: What happened after Franklin made peace with his co-workers by paying the fee?
options: He was fired
He gained influence and changed some of their rules
He was forced to drink beer
He moved back to America immediately
quiz.explanation: Once on a fair footing, he 'soon acquired considerable influence' and carried reasonable changes to their rules.

cards.title: Pay back what you owe, even after you've been let off
cards.body:
Franklin admired Mr. Denham, a merchant who had failed in business in Bristol and settled with his creditors for part of what he owed. Years later, having made a fortune in America, Denham invited those creditors to dinner. Under each plate was an order on a banker for the full remaining balance, with interest.

Legally he owed nothing more. But he chose to make people whole, and earned lasting respect for it. Repaying old debts you could walk away from, even slowly, is one of the strongest ways to show who you are.
cards.quote: every man at the first remove found under his plate an order on a banker for the full amount of the unpaid remainder with interest.
cards.locator: VI. First Visit to London ¶23
cards.apply_it: Is there an old debt or favour you never fully repaid? Make a plan, even a small monthly one, to settle it.

quiz.question: What surprised Mr. Denham's old creditors at his dinner?
options: He asked them for a new loan
He announced he was bankrupt again
He offered them jobs in America
Each found the full unpaid balance, with interest, under his plate
quiz.explanation: Though released from the debt, Denham repaid the full remainder with interest.

cards.title: Sometimes take lower pay for a better future
cards.body:
In London Franklin earned good wages as a compositor. When Denham offered to take him to Philadelphia as a clerk at fifty pounds a year, it was less than he was making. But Denham would teach him bookkeeping and trade, send him on profitable trips, and set him up if he did well. Franklin accepted at once.

A job's value isn't only its salary. Skills, mentors and the doors a role opens can be worth far more than a slightly bigger paycheck now. Compare offers by where they lead in five years, not just next month.
cards.quote: I immediately agreed on the terms of fifty pounds a year, Pennsylvania money; less, indeed, than my present gettings as a compositor, but affording a better prospect.
cards.locator: VI. First Visit to London ¶24
cards.apply_it: For your current job or a new offer, list what you'll learn and who you'll learn from, not just what you'll earn.

quiz.question: Why did Franklin accept a clerk's job that paid less than printing?
options: It offered training and a better prospect
He was tired of London weather
Printing work had dried up
Denham was a relative
quiz.explanation: Franklin chose it because it afforded a better prospect, with training and future opportunities.

cards.title: Call your mistakes 'errata' and set about correcting them
cards.body:
As a printer, Franklin called his life's mistakes 'errata', like misprints to be fixed in a later edition. One was spending money a friend had asked him to collect and hold. Years later, when the friend reminded him, Franklin wrote an honest letter, asked for a little more time, and as soon as he could paid it all back with interest and thanks.

The word is useful. A mistake isn't your whole story; it's an error in the text that you can acknowledge and correct. Owning it plainly and repairing it as fully as possible is what matters.
cards.quote: as soon as I was able, I paid the principal with interest, and many thanks; so that erratum was in some degree corrected.
cards.locator: VII. Beginning Business in Philadelphia ¶36
cards.apply_it: Name one 'erratum' in your past that still bothers you. What is the smallest step you could take to correct it?

quiz.question: How did Franklin handle the money he had wrongly spent for his friend Vernon?
options: He denied ever receiving it
He asked a governor to pay it
He acknowledged it, asked for time, and repaid it with interest
He paid it back in printed books
quiz.explanation: He wrote an honest acknowledgment, asked for patience, and repaid the principal with interest.

cards.title: Don't let professional doom-sayers make your decisions
cards.body:
Soon after Franklin opened his print shop, a grave, wise-looking man named Samuel Mickle stopped by to say he was sorry for him: Philadelphia was sinking, everyone was half-bankrupt, and the new buildings were signs of coming ruin. Franklin was left half melancholy. Mickle kept saying the same for years and refused to buy a house, until he finally paid five times what he could have paid at the start.

Franklin called such people croakers. Some caution is wise, but people who see ruin everywhere can cost you real opportunities if you take them as your guide.
cards.quote: There are croakers in every country, always boding its ruin.
cards.locator: VII. Beginning Business in Philadelphia ¶19
cards.apply_it: Think of a gloomy forecast you've heard repeatedly. Look for evidence for and against it before letting it decide anything for you.

quiz.question: What happened to Samuel Mickle, the 'croaker' who predicted Philadelphia's ruin?
options: He moved away and prospered
He became Franklin's business partner
He was proved right when the city declined
He ended up paying five times the original price for a house
quiz.explanation: He refused to buy for years, then paid five times what the house would have cost when he started croaking.

cards.title: Visible hard work builds trust before your results do
cards.body:
Franklin's new print shop had a printing job paid at a low rate, and he resolved to set a full sheet every day. One night, after finishing, a form broke and two pages scattered; he reset them before going to bed. Neighbours noticed. At a merchants' club where everyone predicted the shop would fail, a doctor said he saw Franklin still at work when he went home and back at work before others were up. Offers of supplies soon followed.

People judge a newcomer by what they see. Consistent, visible effort earns trust and credit early.
cards.quote: I see him still at work when I go home from club, and he is at work again before his neighbors are out of bed.
cards.locator: VII. Beginning Business in Philadelphia ¶29
cards.apply_it: What do the people around you see of your effort? Choose one habit, like punctual delivery, that shows reliability.

quiz.question: What changed the merchants' opinion of Franklin's new print shop?
options: A large government contract
A newspaper advertisement
Visible evidence of his tireless industry
A loan from his father
quiz.explanation: Dr. Baird pointed to Franklin's visible industry, and soon a merchant offered to supply him with stationery.

cards.title: Living for show can sink a promising business
cards.body:
When Franklin's former trainee David Harry set up as a rival printer, with well-connected friends behind him, Franklin feared him and even proposed a partnership. Harry refused with scorn. He dressed like a gentleman, lived expensively, spent his time on amusements, ran into debt and neglected his work. The business left him, and he eventually sold his equipment and went back to farm work.

Advantages at the start mean little if spending races ahead of income and the work itself is neglected. Looking successful is not the same as being successful.
cards.quote: He was very proud, dressed like a gentleman, lived expensively, took much diversion and pleasure abroad, ran in debt, and neglected his business; upon which, all business left him
cards.locator: VIII. Business Success and First Public… ¶7
cards.apply_it: Check your last month: did any spending go mainly to how things look rather than how things work?

quiz.question: Why did David Harry's printing business fail?
options: He lived expensively, ran into debt and neglected his business
Franklin undercut his prices
He had no customers from the start
The government closed it
quiz.explanation: Franklin says Harry dressed and lived expensively, went into debt and neglected his work, so the business left him.

cards.title: Keep a plan quiet until you're ready to act on it
cards.body:
Franklin planned to start a newspaper, and foolishly mentioned it in confidence to George Webb, a printer he hoped to hire later. Webb told Franklin's rival Keimer, who rushed out his own proposal to get in first. Franklin had to scramble, writing pieces for a third paper to draw attention away until Keimer's venture fizzled and Franklin could buy it cheaply.

It worked out, but the lesson stuck: once you share a plan, you no longer control it. Tell people when they need to know, and when you're ready to move.
cards.quote: I foolishly let him know as a secret that I soon intended to begin a newspaper
cards.locator: VII. Beginning Business in Philadelphia ¶31
cards.apply_it: Is there a plan you've been talking about more than acting on? Keep it close until you've taken the first real step.

quiz.question: What went wrong after Franklin told George Webb about his newspaper plan?
options: Webb asked for higher wages
Webb passed it to a rival, who tried to launch a paper first
Webb invested in the paper
Webb published Franklin's essays without permission
quiz.explanation: Webb told Keimer, who immediately published proposals for his own paper to get ahead of Franklin.

cards.title: Remember who helped you first, and pass it on
cards.body:
When Franklin and his partner opened their print shop, every penny had gone on equipment. Then an acquaintance, George House, brought in a countryman looking for a printer. That first customer's five shillings, Franklin wrote, gave him more pleasure than any coin he earned afterwards.

The gratitude lasted. He said it made him readier, perhaps more than was wise, to help young people starting out. A referral, a first order or a word of encouragement means most at the very beginning. Remember who gave you yours, and look for a beginner you can do the same for.
cards.quote: the gratitude I felt toward House has made me often more ready than perhaps I should otherwise have been to assist young beginners.
cards.locator: VII. Beginning Business in Philadelphia ¶18
cards.apply_it: Thank someone who helped you early on. Then refer, hire or encourage one person who is just starting out.

quiz.question: How did George House's small favour affect Franklin's later behaviour?
options: Franklin stopped taking small jobs
Franklin hired House as a partner
Franklin became more ready to help young beginners
Franklin lowered his prices for everyone
quiz.explanation: Franklin said his gratitude to House made him more ready to assist young beginners.

cards.title: When someone treats you unfairly, don't copy them later
cards.body:
Franklin's rival Bradford, as postmaster, forbade the post riders to carry Franklin's newspaper, a petty move that hurt his business. Franklin resented it and thought meanly of him. Years later Franklin himself became postmaster, and he made a point of not repeating the trick; he even says he was satisfied without retaliating.

It's tempting, once you hold power, to pay back old slights. Franklin's choice shows a better use of the memory: let it teach you how not to treat people when your turn comes.
cards.quote: I thought so meanly of him for it, that, when I afterward came into his situation, I took care never to imitate it.
cards.locator: VIII. Business Success and First Public… ¶8
cards.apply_it: Recall an unfair rule or habit someone used against you. If you're ever in their position, what will you do differently?

quiz.question: What did Franklin do when he became postmaster himself?
options: He took care never to imitate Bradford's unfairness
He banned Bradford's newspaper
He sold the post office
He raised postal rates on rivals
quiz.explanation: Franklin says he took care never to imitate Bradford, and was satisfied without retaliating.

cards.title: Get the project done by letting go of the credit
cards.body:
Raising money for Philadelphia's first subscription library, Franklin met resistance whenever he presented it as his own idea; people didn't like helping a neighbour look important. So he put himself out of sight and described it as a plan of 'a number of friends'. Things went far more smoothly, and he used the method for the rest of his life.

He noted that the small sacrifice of vanity is repaid later: if credit goes unclaimed for a while, someone vainer may grab it, and then even envious people will restore it to its true owner.
cards.quote: The present little sacrifice of your vanity will afterwards be amply repaid.
cards.locator: VIII. Business Success and First Public… ¶21
cards.apply_it: For a group project you care about, try presenting it as 'our' idea, not 'mine', and see how people respond.

quiz.question: Why did Franklin present the library as the idea of 'a number of friends'?
options: He was embarrassed by libraries
People resisted helping someone who seemed to raise himself above them
It was legally required
His friends had actually invented it
quiz.explanation: He found that presenting himself as the proposer raised objections, so he stepped out of sight and it went smoothly.

cards.title: An hour or two of study a day can replace a missing education
cards.body:
Franklin left school at ten. Once the subscription library existed, he set aside an hour or two each day for study, and said that this partly made up for the learned education his father had once planned for him. Reading was the only amusement he allowed himself while building his business.

He later received honorary degrees from Harvard and Yale without attending either. A small, steady daily habit of serious reading or study, sustained over years, compounds into real expertise, whatever your formal schooling.
cards.quote: This library afforded me the means of improvement by constant study, for which I set apart an hour or two each day
cards.locator: VIII. Business Success and First Public… ¶22
cards.apply_it: Block a fixed daily study slot, even 30 minutes, and protect it like an appointment for the next month.

quiz.question: How did Franklin make up for leaving school at ten?
options: He hired private tutors
He went to college in London
He studied an hour or two each day using the library
He learned only from his father
quiz.explanation: He set apart an hour or two daily for study, which he said repaired the loss of a learned education.

cards.title: Watch how luxury creeps in, one 'deserved' item at a time
cards.body:
For years Franklin ate breakfast of bread and milk from a cheap earthen bowl with a pewter spoon. One morning he found it in a china bowl with a silver spoon. His wife had bought them, for a large sum, because she felt he deserved them as much as any neighbour. That was the first fine tableware in the house; over the years, as their wealth grew, it grew to hundreds of pounds' worth.

Franklin told the story with affection, but his point was clear: luxury enters gradually, despite good principles. Each upgrade feels deserved; together they reset your normal.
cards.quote: But mark how luxury will enter families, and make a progress, in spite of principle
cards.locator: VIII. Business Success and First Public… ¶23
cards.apply_it: When your income rises, decide in advance what share goes to savings before any upgrades.

quiz.question: What did Franklin's china bowl and silver spoon illustrate?
options: That his wife was wasteful
That silver is a good investment
That you should never accept gifts
How luxury gradually enters a household despite principles
quiz.explanation: He used it to show how luxury enters families and makes progress in spite of principle.

cards.title: Knowing what's right isn't enough; you have to build the habit
cards.body:
Franklin set out, quite confidently, to never do anything wrong. He soon found that while he guarded against one fault another surprised him; habit took advantage of inattention, and inclination was sometimes stronger than reason. He concluded that being convinced you should behave well doesn't stop you slipping.

What works, he decided, is breaking bad habits and deliberately building good ones until they become reliable. That insight, more than any list of virtues, is why his tracking method still appeals: change comes from practice and structure, not good intentions.
cards.quote: the contrary habits must be broken, and good ones acquired and established, before we can have any dependence on a steady, uniform rectitude of conduct.
cards.locator: IX. Plan for Attaining Moral Perfection ¶1
cards.apply_it: Pick one behaviour you already know you should change. Instead of more resolve, design one cue or routine that makes it easier.

quiz.question: What did Franklin conclude after failing to be perfectly good through conviction alone?
options: Good habits must be built and bad ones broken
Virtue is impossible
Only religion can change behaviour
Faults are best ignored
quiz.explanation: He decided that conviction wasn't enough; contrary habits must be broken and good ones established.

cards.title: Talk less, listen more, and learn faster
cards.body:
Franklin's second virtue was Silence: speak only what may benefit others or yourself, and avoid trifling conversation. He placed it early because he wanted to learn while he improved, and he believed knowledge in conversation comes more through the ears than the tongue. He also wanted to break his habit of punning and joking, which he felt only made him welcome among trifling company.

In meetings and social media alike, the urge to fill silence is strong. Listening more lets you learn what others know, and makes what you do say carry more weight.
cards.quote: in conversation it was obtained rather by the use of the ears than of the tongue
cards.locator: IX. Plan for Attaining Moral Perfection ¶29
cards.apply_it: In your next conversation, aim to ask two questions and listen fully before offering your own view.

quiz.question: Why did Franklin rank Silence so high among his virtues?
options: He was shy
He believed knowledge in conversation comes more through listening than talking
Talking was forbidden in print shops
He disliked music
quiz.explanation: He wanted to gain knowledge, which he believed comes by the use of the ears rather than the tongue.

cards.title: Don't let small annoyances and the unavoidable disturb your peace
cards.body:
Tranquillity was the eleventh virtue on Franklin's list, with a simple rule: don't get upset over small things, or over ordinary mishaps nobody could have prevented. Spilled ink, a late delivery, bad weather, a rude stranger: these happen to everyone, and getting upset changes nothing except your own mood.

The skill is sorting events into what deserves your energy and what doesn't. Saving your emotional reactions for things that truly matter, and that you can affect, leaves you calmer and clearer for them.
cards.quote: Be not disturbed at trifles, or at accidents common or unavoidable.
cards.locator: IX. Plan for Attaining Moral Perfection ¶25
cards.apply_it: Next time something small goes wrong, ask: will this matter in a week? If not, let it pass with one slow breath.

quiz.question: What did Franklin's virtue of Tranquillity advise?
options: Avoid all risks
Keep to a strict daily schedule
Don't be disturbed by trifles or unavoidable accidents
Spend time alone each day
quiz.explanation: His precept was: 'Be not disturbed at trifles, or at accidents common or unavoidable.'

cards.title: Resent wrongs less than you think they deserve
cards.body:
Franklin's virtue of Moderation came with a striking instruction: avoid extremes, and hold back from resenting injuries as much as you think they deserve. Not ignoring wrongs, but deliberately responding less than your anger would like.

When we're hurt, our sense of what's fair is usually inflated, and payback tends to escalate. Choosing a smaller response than you feel entitled to keeps conflicts from spiralling, protects relationships, and spares you from carrying anger around. It also leaves room for the other person to make amends.
cards.quote: Avoid extremes; forbear resenting injuries so much as you think they deserve.
cards.locator: IX. Plan for Attaining Moral Perfection ¶21
cards.apply_it: Think of a current grievance. What response would feel fair to you? Now choose something a notch milder.

quiz.question: What did Franklin's Moderation precept say about injuries?
options: Ignore them completely
Repay them exactly
Report them to authorities
Resent them less than you think they deserve
quiz.explanation: The precept was to avoid extremes and 'forbear resenting injuries so much as you think they deserve'.

cards.title: Lose no time, and cut out actions that serve no purpose
cards.body:
Franklin's precept for Industry was short and demanding: lose no time, always be employed in something useful, and cut off all unnecessary actions. He credited industry, together with frugality, for freeing him from debt and building his fortune.

The last part is the most practical today. Much of a busy day goes to motions that add nothing: re-checking feeds, needless meetings, reformatting, waiting without a plan. Trimming these isn't about working every minute; it's about making sure your effort goes to things that matter, so rest can be real rest.
cards.quote: Lose no time; be always employed in something useful; cut off all unnecessary actions.
cards.locator: IX. Plan for Attaining Moral Perfection ¶15
cards.apply_it: List five things you did yesterday that served no real purpose. Choose one to cut out tomorrow.

quiz.question: Which instruction was part of Franklin's precept for Industry?
options: Cut off all unnecessary actions
Work at least twelve hours a day
Never take holidays
Do several tasks at once
quiz.explanation: Industry: 'Lose no time; be always employed in something useful; cut off all unnecessary actions.'

cards.title: Beware the excuse that a 'speckled axe' is good enough
cards.body:
Franklin told of a man who asked a smith to polish his whole axe head bright. The smith agreed if the man turned the grindstone. It was exhausting, and after checking several times the man said he'd take the axe as it was. 'It's only speckled so far,' said the smith. 'Yes,' said the man, 'but I think I like a speckled ax best.'

Franklin saw himself in it when building habits got hard. A voice dressed up as reason suggested that such strictness was silly. Settling can be wise, but notice when 'good enough' is just fatigue talking.
cards.quote: ‘Yes,’ says the man, ‘but I think I like a speckled ax best.’
cards.locator: IX. Plan for Attaining Moral Perfection ¶59
cards.apply_it: Think of a goal you've recently decided wasn't worth finishing. Was that a real judgement, or were you just tired of turning the wheel?

quiz.question: What does the 'speckled axe' story warn against?
options: Buying cheap tools
Trusting blacksmiths
Working too hard on details
Giving up on improvement and calling it a preference
quiz.explanation: The man tired of turning the grindstone and declared he liked a speckled axe best, as people do when habit change gets hard.

cards.title: Pride is the hardest habit to beat, so expect it to resurface
cards.body:
Franklin added Humility to his list after a Quaker friend told him he was seen as proud and overbearing. He admitted he never really acquired the virtue, only its appearance. Pride, he wrote, is perhaps the hardest natural passion to subdue: disguise it, fight it, stifle it, and it still pops up. Even if he had overcome it, he joked, he'd probably be proud of his humility.

That honesty is useful. Rather than assuming you've conquered ego, stay alert for its quieter forms: needing to be right, fishing for credit, feeling superior about being modest.
cards.quote: even if I could conceive that I had completely overcome it, I should probably be proud of my humility.
cards.locator: IX. Plan for Attaining Moral Perfection ¶68
cards.apply_it: Ask a trusted friend where your pride shows up most. Listen without defending yourself.

quiz.question: What did Franklin say would happen even if he fully overcame pride?
options: He would probably be proud of his humility
He would lose his ambition
He would become a better speaker
His friends would trust him less
quiz.explanation: He joked that if he conquered pride, he would probably be proud of his humility.

cards.title: Honesty is rare, which makes it a poor person's best asset
cards.body:
Franklin argued that bad actions aren't harmful because they're forbidden; they're forbidden because they're harmful. So being good is in everyone's interest, even for happiness in this world. He planned to tell young people a practical truth: merchants, nobles, states and rulers always need honest people to manage their affairs, and such people are rare.

That scarcity is an opportunity. Skill can be hired anywhere; proven integrity can't. Being reliably honest with money and promises makes you the person people want to trust with more.
cards.quote: no qualities were so likely to make a poor man's fortune as those of probity and integrity.
cards.locator: IX. Plan for Attaining Moral Perfection ¶64
cards.apply_it: Where at work could you show integrity in a visible way this week, such as admitting an error or returning extra change?

quiz.question: Why did Franklin think honesty could make a poor person's fortune?
options: Honest people pay less tax
The powerful always need honest people to manage their affairs, and they are rare
Honesty is required by law
Honest people inherit more
quiz.explanation: He said rich merchants, nobles, states and princes need honest instruments, and such people are rare.

cards.title: One capable person with a good plan and focus can do great things
cards.body:
Franklin once dreamed of a worldwide society of people committed to virtue. Business and public duties meant it never happened, but he kept one conviction from it: he was never discouraged by the size of an undertaking, because one person of ordinary ability can achieve great changes if they first form a good plan and then cut away distractions to make carrying it out their main business.

His own life showed it: libraries, fire companies, a hospital, an academy. Big goals become workable with a clear plan and ruthless focus.
cards.quote: one man of tolerable abilities may work great changes, and accomplish great affairs among mankind, if he first forms a good plan
cards.locator: IX. Plan for Attaining Moral Perfection ¶90
cards.apply_it: Write a one-page plan for something ambitious you care about. Then name one distraction you'll cut to make room for it.

quiz.question: What two things did Franklin say let an ordinary person accomplish great things?
options: Wealth and connections
Luck and charm
A good plan and cutting out distractions
Education and family support
quiz.explanation: He said a person of tolerable abilities can work great changes by forming a good plan and making it their sole study.

cards.title: Refuse to spread personal attacks, even when asked
cards.body:
As a newspaper owner, Franklin was often asked to print attacks on people, with writers claiming freedom of the press. His answer: he'd print the piece separately and the author could distribute it himself, but he wouldn't spread the abuse to subscribers who had paid for useful or entertaining reading. He warned that printers who traded in false accusations stirred hatred, even duels.

Today everyone with a phone has a press. You can't stop people writing nasty things, but you can choose not to forward, repost or amplify them.
cards.quote: I would not take upon me to spread his detraction
cards.locator: X. Poor Richard’s Almanac and Other… ¶4
cards.apply_it: Before you share a post or message criticising someone, ask: is it true, is it useful, and would I say it to their face?

quiz.question: How did Franklin handle requests to print personal attacks in his newspaper?
options: He printed them for a higher fee
He refused to spread them, but offered to print them separately for the author
He forwarded them to the courts
He printed them anonymously
quiz.explanation: He would print the piece separately for the author to distribute, but would not spread the detraction through his paper.

cards.title: Everyone in a family business should be able to keep the accounts
cards.body:
Franklin's printing partner in Charleston was honest but hopeless with accounts. When he died, his widow, raised in Holland where she had learned bookkeeping, sent Franklin clear statements every quarter, ran the business successfully, raised her children and bought the print shop for her son.

Franklin used her story to urge that girls be taught accounts rather than only music and dancing, so they could protect themselves from crafty people and keep a business going. The wider lesson holds for any household: everyone who might need to run things should understand the numbers.
cards.quote: she not only sent me as clear a state as she could find of the transactions past, but continued to account with the greatest regularity and exactness every quarter afterwards
cards.locator: X. Poor Richard’s Almanac and Other… ¶5
cards.apply_it: Make sure at least two people in your household or business can read the accounts and know where the key documents are.

quiz.question: What allowed the Charleston widow to keep the printing business going?
options: Franklin managed it for her
She sold it immediately
She hired a manager from London
She had learned to keep accounts and did so exactly
quiz.explanation: Trained in accounts, she reported with regularity and exactness, ran the business well, and bought it for her son.

cards.title: Turn a distraction into a study game with stakes
cards.body:
While learning Italian, Franklin had a friend who kept tempting him into chess, which ate the time he wanted for study. So he set a condition: the winner of each game could assign the loser a task, like memorising grammar or doing translations, to be completed on honour before they next met. Since they were evenly matched, they 'beat one another into that language'.

If you can't drop a pastime, attach your goal to it. A friendly bet, a shared challenge or a small penalty can turn wasted hours into progress.
cards.quote: As we played pretty equally, we thus beat one another into that language.
cards.locator: X. Poor Richard’s Almanac and Other… ¶9
cards.apply_it: Pair a pastime you enjoy with a learning goal: for example, the loser of tonight's game learns ten new words or reads a chapter.

quiz.question: How did Franklin stop chess from eating into his Italian study?
options: The winner of each game set the loser a study task
He gave up chess entirely
He only played on Sundays
He studied while his friend made moves
quiz.explanation: Each game's winner could impose a grammar or translation task on the loser, so they learned Italian together.

cards.title: Spell out everything in a partnership agreement up front
cards.body:
Franklin set up several of his journeymen as printers in other colonies under partnership deals, and most did well enough to buy him out after six years. He noted that partnerships often end in quarrels, yet all of his ended amicably. The reason, he believed, was that every duty and expectation was settled explicitly in writing, leaving nothing to dispute.

However much partners trust each other at the start, small jealousies about who works harder can grow. Clear written terms on roles, money and exit protect both the business and the friendship.
cards.quote: Partnerships often finish in quarrels; but I was happy in this, that mine were all carried on and ended amicably
cards.locator: XI. Interest in Public Affairs ¶16
cards.apply_it: If you share a business, rent or project with anyone, write down who does what, who pays what, and how either can leave.

quiz.question: Why did Franklin's partnerships end amicably when many others ended in quarrels?
options: He chose only family members
He kept them very short
Everything expected from each partner was settled explicitly in advance
He always took the smaller share
quiz.explanation: He credited the precaution of explicitly settling in their articles everything to be done by or expected from each partner.

cards.title: Prepare people's minds before you ask for their support
cards.body:
Dr. Thomas Bond wanted to found a hospital in Philadelphia, but the idea was new and few would subscribe. He came to Franklin, who liked the plan, gave money himself, and did what Bond had skipped: before asking anyone, he wrote about the subject in the newspapers so people understood it. Donations then came far more freely.

Franklin used this approach repeatedly, for the academy and city reforms too. People resist what's unfamiliar. Explain the problem and the idea first, give them time, and the request lands on prepared ground.
cards.quote: Previously, however, to the solicitation, I endeavoured to prepare the minds of the people by writing on the subject in the newspapers, which was my usual custom in such cases
cards.locator: XIII. Public Services and Duties (1749⁠–⁠1753) ¶14
cards.apply_it: Before your next big request at work or home, share the background and reasoning a few days ahead, then ask.

quiz.question: What did Franklin do that Dr. Bond had not, when raising money for the hospital?
options: Offered donors free treatment
Asked only wealthy people
Prepared people's minds by writing about it first
Hid his own involvement completely
quiz.explanation: Franklin first wrote about the subject in the newspapers to prepare people's minds, his usual custom.

cards.title: Happiness comes more from small daily advantages than big windfalls
cards.body:
Franklin defended his attention to seemingly trivial things like street sweeping. Dust in one person's eye is minor; multiplied across a city every day, it matters. Human happiness, he wrote, comes less from rare strokes of great fortune than from small advantages that occur daily.

His example: teach a poor young man to shave himself and keep his razor sharp, and you may do more for his happiness than by giving him a thousand guineas. The money would soon be spent; the skill would save him trouble and give him small pleasure for life.
cards.quote: Human felicity is produced not so much by great pieces of good fortune that seldom happen, as by little advantages that occur every day.
cards.locator: XIII. Public Services and Duties (1749⁠–⁠1753) ¶30
cards.apply_it: Name one small daily friction in your life. Fix it this week, whether with a tool, a skill or a routine.

quiz.question: Why did Franklin think teaching a man to shave could beat giving him a thousand guineas?
options: Shaving was a well-paid trade
The money would soon be spent, but the skill gives daily benefit for life
Guineas were losing value
Barbers were dishonest
quiz.explanation: He said the money may soon be spent, but the skill gives daily convenience and pleasure for life.

cards.title: Winning arguments can cost you the goodwill you actually need
cards.body:
When his friend Robert Morris became governor, Franklin advised him that he could have a comfortable term if he simply avoided disputes with the Assembly. Morris laughed that he loved disputing; his father had trained his children to argue at the dinner table for fun. Franklin thought that training unwise. In his experience, people who habitually dispute and contradict tend to do badly in their affairs: they sometimes win the point but never win goodwill.

Morris's term turned into a running battle. Being right is satisfying; being someone people want to work with is usually more useful.
cards.quote: They get victory sometimes, but they never get good will, which would be of more use to them.
cards.locator: XV. Quarrels with the Proprietary Governors ¶1
cards.apply_it: In your next disagreement, ask yourself which matters more here: winning this point or keeping this person's goodwill?

quiz.question: What did Franklin observe about people who love disputing and contradicting?
options: They become great lawyers
They are usually right
They make the best leaders
They win victories but not goodwill
quiz.explanation: Franklin said such people 'get victory sometimes, but they never get good will, which would be of more use to them'.

cards.title: Fight hard over issues without making it personal
cards.body:
For years Franklin led the Assembly's side against Governor Morris, writing sharp, sometimes abusive replies to his messages. You might expect the two men to hate each other. Instead they often dined together, and Morris would consult Franklin on difficult points. Franklin guessed that Morris, trained as a lawyer, saw them both as advocates for different clients rather than personal enemies.

That's a valuable frame at work, in politics or in a family. You can oppose someone's position firmly while still respecting them, which keeps the door open for cooperation when interests align.
cards.quote: Notwithstanding the continual wrangle between the governor and the House, in which I, as a member, had so large a share, there still subsisted a civil intercourse between that gentleman and myself, and we never had any personal difference.
cards.locator: XVII. Franklin’s Defense of the Frontier ¶16
cards.apply_it: Think of someone you disagree with on an important issue. Find one occasion to be friendly with them that has nothing to do with the dispute.

quiz.question: How did Franklin explain Governor Morris's lack of personal resentment toward him?
options: Morris saw them both as advocates for different clients
Morris had not read Franklin's replies
They were secretly business partners
Morris planned to resign anyway
quiz.explanation: Franklin thought that, being a lawyer, Morris saw them as advocates for contending clients rather than enemies.

cards.title: People are happiest when they have useful work to do
cards.body:
While building a frontier fort in rough winter weather, Franklin noticed a pattern among his men. On working days they were cheerful and good-natured, and spent the evening in good spirits after a solid day's work. On idle days, when rain stopped work, they grew quarrelsome, complaining about the pork and the bread. It reminded him of a sea captain who, when told there was nothing left to do, ordered the crew to scour the anchor.

Having meaningful work, not just rest, is a big part of wellbeing. Long empty stretches often breed irritability.
cards.quote: when men are employed, they are best contented; for on the days they worked they were good-natured and cheerful
cards.locator: XVII. Franklin’s Defense of the Frontier ¶7
cards.apply_it: On your next free day, plan one satisfying, useful task alongside your rest, and notice how your mood compares.

quiz.question: What did Franklin observe about his soldiers on idle days?
options: They rested and became healthier
They wrote letters home
They studied military tactics
They became quarrelsome and found fault with everything
quiz.explanation: On idle days they were mutinous and quarrelsome, finding fault with their pork and bread.

cards.title: Don't plan the celebration before the result is in
cards.body:
Before news came of General Braddock's attack on Fort Duquesne, two doctors asked Franklin to help fund fireworks for the expected victory. He declined, saying there would be time to prepare for rejoicing once they knew there was something to rejoice about; the events of war are always uncertain. The doctors were surprised. Then news arrived of Braddock's crushing defeat, and they were spared the embarrassment of fireworks for a disaster.

Whether it's a job offer, a deal or an exam, spending on the celebration before the outcome is confirmed is a needless risk.
cards.quote: it would, I thought, be time enough to prepare for the rejoicing when we knew we should have occasion to rejoice.
cards.locator: XVI. Braddock’s Expedition ¶27
cards.apply_it: Is there any spending or announcement you're planning ahead of a result that isn't confirmed? Wait until it is.

quiz.question: Why did Franklin refuse to fund the victory fireworks?
options: He disliked fireworks
The outcome of the battle was still uncertain
He had no money
Fireworks were illegal
quiz.explanation: He said there would be time to prepare for rejoicing once they knew they had reason to, since war is uncertain.

cards.title: Contempt for local knowledge is a costly kind of overconfidence
cards.body:
General Braddock was brave, Franklin wrote, but had too much self-confidence and too low an opinion of American colonists and Native Americans. He slighted the Native American guides who could have scouted for him, and they left. When Franklin cautiously warned that a long, thin column on a narrow forest road was vulnerable to ambush, Braddock smiled at his ignorance. Weeks later the army was ambushed and routed, with most of its officers killed or wounded.

Experts can be wrong outside the conditions they know. Leaders who dismiss people with local experience lose exactly the information they most need.
cards.quote: But he had too much self-confidence, too high an opinion of the validity of regular troops, and too mean a one of both Americans and Indians.
cards.locator: XVI. Braddock’s Expedition ¶18
cards.apply_it: On your next project, find the person closest to the ground, a customer or junior colleague, and ask what could go wrong.

quiz.question: According to Franklin, what flaw contributed most to General Braddock's defeat?
options: Overconfidence and contempt for local people and their knowledge
Too few soldiers
Lack of courage
Bad weather
quiz.explanation: Franklin said Braddock had too much self-confidence and too low an opinion of American colonists and Native Americans, and slighted his guides.

cards.title: Spend your time on new work, not defending old work
cards.body:
When the French scientist Abbé Nollet published a book attacking Franklin's electrical experiments, Franklin started a reply, then stopped. His experiments could be repeated by anyone; if they held up, they needed no defence, and if they didn't, no argument could save them. A dispute across languages would drag on through mistranslations. He decided it was better to spend his limited time making new experiments than arguing about old ones.

Others defended him, and his views were widely adopted. Often the best answer to criticism is better work, not a long rebuttal.
cards.quote: I concluded to let my papers shift for themselves, believing it was better to spend what time I could spare from public business in making new experiments, than in disputing about those already made.
cards.locator: XVIII. Scientific Experiments ¶6
cards.apply_it: Is there an argument you're tempted to keep fighting online or at work? Put that time into your next piece of work instead.

quiz.question: Why did Franklin never answer the Abbé Nollet's attacks?
options: He agreed with Nollet
He was forbidden by the Royal Society
He couldn't read French
He thought new experiments were a better use of time than disputes
quiz.explanation: He let his papers 'shift for themselves', preferring to spend time making new experiments rather than disputing old ones.

cards.title: Looking busy isn't the same as getting things done
cards.body:
Lord Loudoun, commander of the British army in America, kept ships and messengers waiting for weeks for letters that were 'always to be ready tomorrow'. Visitors always found him at his desk, pen in hand, and assumed he must be writing a great deal. A messenger who had called every morning for a fortnight summed him up: like St. George on inn signs, always on horseback and never riding on.

Franklin noted that London eventually replaced him partly because ministers never heard what he was doing. Activity that never ships is invisible to everyone who depends on you.
cards.quote: ‘Yes,’ says Innis, ‘but he is like St. George on the signs, always on horseback, and never rides on.’
cards.locator: XIX. Agent of Pennsylvania in London ¶8
cards.apply_it: Look at your task list. What have you been 'working on' for weeks without finishing? Ship a version of it this week.

quiz.question: What did the messenger mean by 'always on horseback, and never rides on'?
options: Loudoun travelled too much
Loudoun always seemed busy but never delivered
Loudoun was a skilled rider
Loudoun refused to leave New York
quiz.explanation: Loudoun appeared constantly at work, yet his letters were never ready, so nothing moved forward.

cards.title: Everyone thinks they alone are out of the fog
cards.body:
Franklin admired a small religious group, the Dunkers, who refused to publish a fixed creed because they kept discovering that some of their beliefs were mistaken and feared freezing their errors in print. He contrasted this with groups sure they held all truth, comparing them to a traveller in fog: he sees the people ahead, behind and in the fields wrapped in mist, while around himself everything looks clear, though he's as deep in the fog as they are.

It's a vivid picture of a universal bias. Holding your views a little more loosely leaves room to learn.
cards.quote: like a man traveling in foggy weather ... near him all appears clear, though in truth he is as much in the fog as any of them.
cards.locator: XII. Defense of the Province ¶16
cards.apply_it: Pick one strong opinion you hold. Write down what evidence would change your mind, and seek some out.

quiz.question: What point was Franklin making with the traveller in the fog?
options: We tend to see others as confused while assuming our own view is clear
Travel is dangerous in bad weather
Groups should stay together
Leaders must walk ahead of followers
quiz.explanation: The traveller sees everyone else in fog but thinks all is clear around him, though he is just as deep in it.

cards.title: The first savings are the hardest; after that money grows faster
cards.body:
As his newspaper and printing business prospered, Franklin noticed the truth of an old saying: once you have your first hundred pounds, the second comes more easily. Money, he wrote, is prolific by nature: capital lets you take on bigger jobs, buy materials more cheaply, lend at interest and survive slow months.

That's why the start feels so slow and discouraging. The first emergency fund or the first business capital takes the most sacrifice. Once it exists, it begins working alongside you, and progress speeds up.
cards.quote: ‘that after getting the first hundred pound, it is more easy to get the second,’ money itself being of a prolific nature.
cards.locator: XI. Interest in Public Affairs ¶15
cards.apply_it: Set a clear first savings milestone and protect it. Remind yourself that the slowest part comes first.

quiz.question: Why did Franklin say the second hundred pounds comes more easily than the first?
options: Prices fall over time
Banks reward loyal customers
Taxes are lower on the second hundred
Money is of a prolific nature and helps make more money
quiz.explanation: Franklin explained it by 'money itself being of a prolific nature'.
